statement: An L-tile is a 2 by 2 square with one small square missing. Tiles may be turned. Which rectangle can be covered exactly by L-tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps?

choices.misconception: I matched the 3 squares of the rectangle to the 3 squares of one tile, without checking that an L fits in a strip one square wide.
I checked that 6 squares make exactly two tiles and did not notice that a strip one square wide has no room for an L.
I thought any rectangle two squares tall would work because the tiles are two squares tall, but 8 squares cannot be split into tiles of 3.
I checked that 9 squares make exactly three tiles, but each corner of the 3 by 3 needs its own tile, and four corners need more than three tiles.

hints: Count the squares first: the total must be a multiple of 3.
Tiling: the area is only the first test. After that, look at tight spots, such as narrow strips and corners, where an L-tile may not fit at all.
A strip one square wide holds no L-tile, 8 is not a multiple of 3, and in the 3 by 3 every corner needs a tile of its own.

solutions.reliable: Area first: each tile covers 3 squares, so the area must divide by 3. The 2 by 4 has 8 squares and fails. The 1 by 3 and the 1 by 6 are only one square wide, and an L-tile always needs two rows and two columns, so they fail. The 3 by 3 has area 9, so it would need exactly 3 tiles, but any tile placed inside it can touch at most one of its 4 corners, so 3 tiles cannot cover all 4 corners. The 2 by 3 works: one tile covers the two top-left squares and the bottom-left square, and a second tile, turned halfway round, covers the other three. The transferable idea: the right area is needed but is not enough; check that the shape fits in the tightest spots.

whyOnTest: Tiling questions often pass the area test and still fail, so this probes whether a solver checks the shape and not just the count.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
